headline: Apple's First Folding iPhone May Cost $2,000 and Be Called the 'iPhone Duo'

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Apple is a company that makes phones, tablets, and computers. For a long time, people have heard rumors that Apple was making a new kind of iPhone that can fold in half, like a book. Now, a news reporter named Mark Gurman says this new phone might be called the 'iPhone Duo.' It could cost about $2,000 for the basic version, which is a lot more than a regular iPhone. A fancier version with more storage space (room to save photos, videos, and apps) could cost around $3,000. The phone might come in white and dark blue colors and could go on sale in October. People think it will let you use two apps at the same time on its folded screen, kind of like using an iPad. Apple has not said anything official yet, but a big event is happening soon where they might share more details. This matters because folding phones are still new and exciting, and Apple is one of the biggest phone makers in the world.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: For years, people have wondered if Apple would ever make a folding iPhone, similar to folding phones already made by other companies like Samsung and Google. Now, according to reporter Mark Gurman, Apple's folding phone finally has a possible name: the 'iPhone Duo.' Interestingly, this name has been used before—Microsoft called its own folding device the 'Surface Duo,' and Google once used 'Duo' for a video-calling app that didn't last very long. The rumored iPhone Duo is expected to start at $2,000 for a version with 256 gigabytes of storage (a measurement of how much data, like photos and apps, a phone can hold). A model with much more storage, up to 2 terabytes, could cost close to $3,000. That price would make it pricier than some folding phones from Google and Samsung, but slightly cheaper than Samsung's most expensive folding model. The phone is expected to launch in October in two colors, white and dark blue. It's also rumored to let users run two iPhone apps side by side, multitask like on an iPad, and use an Apple Pencil for writing or drawing. This news comes right before Apple's big product launch event, which will be its first since a new CEO, John Ternus, took charge. Nothing is official yet, but if these rumors are true, it would be one of Apple's biggest and most expensive product launches in years, and it could push other phone companies to improve their own folding phones too.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Rumors about an Apple folding phone have circulated for years, but new details reported by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman suggest the device may finally be close to launching—and it might carry a familiar name. According to the report, Apple's first folding iPhone could be called the 'iPhone Duo,' even though that name was previously used by Microsoft for its Surface Duo devices and briefly by Google for a video chat app that later shut down. Before this report, the device had mostly been referred to by its rumored codename, 'iPhone Ultra.' The report claims the phone will start at $2,000 for a 256GB storage model, with a top-tier version offering up to 2TB of storage priced around $3,000. That starting price would place it above the cheapest folding phones from competitors—Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 both start at $1,899—but below Samsung's premium Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which costs $2,099.99. If accurate, this pricing shows how competitive and expensive the foldable phone market has become, with major tech companies racing to offer bigger screens, better multitasking, and more storage. The iPhone Duo is expected to ship as early as October, in white and dark blue color options. Rumored features include the ability to run two iPhone apps side by side, iPad-style multitasking, and support for the Apple Pencil stylus, which is currently only compatible with iPads. These features suggest Apple wants the folding iPhone to blur the line between phone and tablet, giving users more flexibility for work, creativity, and entertainment. This report arrives just hours before Apple's iPhone launch event, notably the first major product event since John Ternus became CEO. Because nothing has been confirmed by Apple itself, all of these details—the name, price, and release date—remain speculation based on insider sourcing until the company makes an official announcement.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: After years of speculation, a new report from Bloomberg journalist Mark Gurman claims Apple's long-awaited folding iPhone finally has a name, a price, and a release timeline—though none of this has been confirmed by Apple itself. According to the report, the device may be called the 'iPhone Duo,' a name that carries some baggage: Microsoft already used 'Surface Duo' for its own dual-screen devices, and Google briefly used 'Duo' for a now-discontinued video calling app. Before this leak, most rumors referred to the device as the 'iPhone Ultra.' Gurman's report states the phone will start at $2,000 for a version with 256GB of storage, while a top-tier model with up to 2TB of storage could cost around $3,000. This pricing places Apple's foldable in an interesting spot within the growing foldable phone market. It would be more expensive than the base models of Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, both of which start at $1,899, but cheaper than Samsung's high-end Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, priced at $2,099.99. This positioning suggests Apple may be aiming for a premium, but not necessarily the most expensive, spot in the foldable market—a strategy it has used before with other product lines. The report also claims the phone will ship as soon as October, available in white and dark blue colors. In terms of features, previous rumors—reinforced by this report—suggest the device will support running two iPhone apps simultaneously side by side, offer iPad-style multitasking capabilities, and work with the Apple Pencil stylus, a tool historically reserved for iPads. If true, these features would mark a significant shift for the iPhone, blending functionality that currently separates phones from tablets. This kind of device could appeal to students, professionals, and creators who want a more powerful, flexible tool in their pocket, though the high price would likely put it out of reach for many everyday consumers. The timing of this report is also notable: it arrived just hours before Apple's iPhone launch event, the first since John Ternus took over as CEO. Because these details come from an unofficial, insider source rather than Apple's own announcement, they should be treated as reliable rumors rather than confirmed facts until Apple presents official information at its event.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Speculation about an Apple foldable device has persisted for years, but a new report from Bloomberg's Mark Gurman—published just hours before Apple's iPhone launch event—claims to reveal key details: a name, a price structure, and a rough shipping timeline for the company's first folding iPhone. According to the report, the device may be branded the 'iPhone Duo,' a notable departure from its previous rumored codename, 'iPhone Ultra.' The name choice is somewhat unusual given its history: Microsoft used 'Surface Duo' for its own dual-screen smartphones, and Google briefly applied 'Duo' to a video-calling app that was eventually discontinued and folded into Google Meet. Whether Apple's use of the name reflects confidence, coincidence, or indifference to past associations remains unclear until an official announcement is made. On pricing, the report suggests the iPhone Duo will start at $2,000 for a 256GB storage configuration, with a higher-end model offering up to 2TB of storage priced around $3,000. This pricing strategy positions Apple within a competitive and rapidly maturing foldable phone market. For comparison, Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 both start at a lower $1,899, while Samsung's premium Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs slightly more at $2,099.99. By pricing its device between these competitors, Apple may be signaling an attempt to position the iPhone Duo as a premium—but not necessarily top-of-market—option, a pricing approach the company has used historically to balance exclusivity with broader appeal. The report also indicates a possible shipping window as early as October, with color options limited to white and dark blue at launch. In terms of functionality, the report reinforces earlier rumors: the device is expected to support running two iPhone apps simultaneously in a side-by-side view, offer multitasking capabilities similar to the iPad, and support the Apple Pencil stylus—a tool that has, until now, been exclusive to Apple's tablet lineup. If accurate, these features suggest Apple intends to merge certain iPad-like productivity functions into its phone lineup, potentially reshaping how consumers think about the boundaries between smartphones and tablets. Such a shift could have ripple effects across the tech industry, pushing competitors to further refine their own foldable offerings and potentially accelerating consumer adoption of foldable technology more broadly, despite its historically high price point limiting mainstream accessibility. It's worth noting that all of these details originate from a single, though generally well-regarded, insider source rather than an official Apple statement. Given that the report was published just hours before Apple's own launch event—the first major product reveal since John Ternus became CEO—it's likely that concrete, verified details will emerge shortly. Until then, this information should be treated as a highly plausible leak rather than confirmed fact, illustrating how much anticipation and industry-watching surrounds even the smallest hints of Apple's next major product category.

questions: If a folding phone like this costs $2,000 or more, who do you think would actually buy one, and how might that affect what phones become popular in schools or among your friends?
Apple might reuse a name ('Duo') that other companies have already used. Why do you think company names and branding matter so much in the tech world?
If phones start doing more of what tablets and laptops can do, how might that change the way students use technology for schoolwork in the future?
